title: Background radiation & safety
examples: Where does background radiation come from in our environment?
What is the difference between contamination and irradiation?
What are the main safety rules when dealing with radiation?

explain.say: Today we will learn about background radiation and safety.
Natural sources create background radiation around us.
We must also consider man-made sources of radiation.
Contamination means radioactive material is on your skin or clothes.
Irradiation means the material is passing through your body.
For safety, we use distance, time, and shielding always.

faq.a: It is the natural level of radiation present in our environment all the time. It comes from sources like the ground and space. You might also hear it called 'natural background radiation' or 'ambient radiation levels'.
asks: Where does this background radiation come from?

faq.q: How do I tell if I have radiation contamination?
faq.a: You need special equipment like a Geiger counter to check for it. If it is on your skin, you should wash thoroughly. Other ways to ask are: 'Is my skin dirty with radiation?' or 'How do I check for radioactive dust?'
asks: Do I need a special tool to check for it?
What if I think I am contaminated?

faq.q: What is the difference between contamination and irradiation?
faq.a: Contamination means the material is physically on you, like dust. Irradiation means the energy is passing through you, like an X-ray beam. Students might ask: 'Is it on me or passing through me?' or 'What is the difference between surface and beam radiation?'
asks: Is it stuck on me or going through me?

faq.q: Why is distance important for radiation safety?
faq.a: Radiation intensity decreases rapidly as you move away from the source. Being further away significantly reduces the amount of radiation you receive. You could ask: 'Does being far away help?' or 'How much does distance matter?'
asks: How far away should I be?

faq.q: What is shielding in radiation safety?
faq.a: Shielding involves using materials to block or absorb radiation. Dense materials like lead are often used for this purpose. You might ask: 'What blocks radiation?' or 'What materials are good shields?'
asks: What do I use to shield myself?

facts: Background radiation comes from natural sources like rocks and space.
Contamination means radioactive material is physically present on a surface.
Irradiation means radiation passes through the body from a source.
Safety measures include maximizing distance, minimizing time, and using shielding.

quiz.say: If radioactive dust settles on your jacket, this is an example of:
quiz.why: Contamination means the material is physically resting on the surface, like dust on your jacket.

wrong.0: Shielding is a protective action, not the type of exposure.
wrong.1: Background refers to the natural level, not the specific type of exposure.
wrong.3: Irradiation describes energy passing through you, not resting on you.

quiz.say: To reduce radiation dose, you should:
quiz.why: Increasing distance or decreasing time are two of the three main ways to reduce radiation exposure.

wrong.0: Staying close maximizes the intensity of the radiation received.
wrong.2: Spending more time near a source increases the total dose received.
wrong.3: Less shielding means more radiation reaches your body.

quiz.say: The primary source of background radiation from Earth's crust is:
quiz.why: Uranium and Thorium are naturally occurring radioactive elements found in rocks and the Earth's crust.

wrong.0: Man-made sources are separate from the natural background radiation we are discussing.
wrong.2: X-rays are artificial sources used in medicine, not background sources.
wrong.3: Cosmic rays are only one part; the Earth's crust is another major source.
